name: Setmelanotide

lead: Setmelanotide (Imcivree) is a melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonist from Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, given by daily injection. It is approved for severe obesity caused by specific rare genetic conditions, including POMC, PCSK1 and LEPR deficiency and Bardet-Biedl syndrome.

It is a rare-disease therapy rather than a general weight-loss drug, and no established role has been shown for people whose obesity has common causes. It appears in looksmaxxing discussions mainly as an example of targeted pharmacology.

paras: Setmelanotide stimulates MC4R in the hypothalamus, a key point in the leptin-melanocortin pathway that controls hunger and energy expenditure. In people whose genetic defect disrupts upstream signalling, direct MC4R activation can restore satiety signalling and reduce hunger.

Common effects include injection-site reactions, skin darkening, nausea and spontaneous penile erections or sexual arousal effects, and depression and suicidal ideation are monitored. It is prescription-only and approved only for confirmed genetic diagnoses, so use for ordinary obesity is off-label and has no supporting evidence.

lead: Setmelanotide, sold as Imcivree, is a melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonist given by daily subcutaneous injection. It was invented at Ipsen and developed by Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, and it is approved for obesity caused by rare genetic or acquired disorders of the leptin-melanocortin pathway [1][2]. It was approved in the United States in November 2020 and in the European Union in July 2021 and the FDA considers it first-in-class [1].

The current US label covers adults and children with acquired hypothalamic obesity (aged 4 and over) and with syndromic or monogenic obesity due to Bardet-Biedl syndrome or genetically confirmed POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (aged 2 and over) [2]. It is not approved for ordinary polygenic obesity [1].

Setmelanotide is not a general weight-loss drug, and the sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion of it. It is included because it is an example of targeted pharmacology in the obesity field.

paras: The US label indicates setmelanotide to reduce excess body weight and maintain reduction long term in people with acquired hypothalamic obesity, Bardet-Biedl syndrome, or POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency confirmed by genetic testing [2]. An earlier approval described by Wikipedia covered the three monogenic conditions in people aged six and over, and notes it is not approved for variants classified benign, other genetic syndromes or common obesity [1].

There is no approved or studied appearance use. Wikipedia notes the drug has some efficacy in people without the approved genetic variants but that safety and efficacy in that wider population are not well understood [1].

In two open-label one-year studies, most participants with POMC/PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency lost more than 10 percent of body weight, and some reported less hunger [1][3]. A 2016 report described treatment of POMC deficiency with an MC4R agonist and a 2018 report described durable weight loss in three people with leptin receptor deficiency [4][5]. A phase 3 trial in Bardet-Biedl and Alström syndromes had a 14-week double-blind period followed by a 52-week open-label period [6]. A phase 2 open-label trial and a 2026 phase 3 trial studied acquired hypothalamic obesity [7][8]. The VENTURE trial examined children aged 2 to 5 [9]. A trial in Prader-Willi syndrome showed no benefit, according to Wikipedia [1][10].

Common effects include injection-site reactions, skin hyperpigmentation, headache and gastrointestinal effects [1]. The label lists disturbance in sexual arousal (spontaneous erections in males and sexual reactions in females, with an erection over four hours needing emergency care), depression and suicidal ideation, hypersensitivity, darkening of existing nevi and new nevi, and acute adrenal insufficiency in acquired hypothalamic obesity [2]. The label advises discontinuing during pregnancy unless benefits outweigh risks [2].

Setmelanotide is an MC4 receptor agonist with about 20-fold lower activity at MC3 and MC1 receptors. MC4 receptors in the hypothalamus regulate hunger, satiety and energy expenditure, and the drug is thought to restore pathway activity in people whose upstream signaling is impaired [2][1]. Unlike some earlier MC4 agonists it has not been found to raise heart rate or blood pressure [1]. It is a cyclic peptide [1]; reviews place it within the leptin-melanocortin pathway field [11][12].

Setmelanotide was invented at Ipsen under names including BIM-22493 and RM-493, and Rhythm Pharmaceuticals developed it; the FDA gave it orphan, breakthrough and priority review designations [1]. Wikipedia reports a 2021 price of $330 for a 1 mg daily dose [1]. Its first approval is reviewed in Drugs [13].

Human trials include POMC and LEPR deficiency phase 3 studies, a Bardet-Biedl/Alström phase 3 trial, MC4R deficiency work and acquired hypothalamic obesity trials from phase 2 to phase 3 [3][6][14][7][8]. Studies in children aged 2 to 5 and extension studies have also been reported [9][15]. No published trial has tested setmelanotide for facial appearance or in people with common obesity.
